title: Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench: Testing the Limits of Agents on Long-Horizon Terminal Tasks
hook: 46 terminal tasks that take hours, not minutes — and today's best agent still only nails 15% of them, with the average model managing barely 4%.
key_points: 46 long-horizon terminal tasks spanning 9 categories — experiment reproduction, software engineering, scientific computing, and more.
Each task is decomposed into fine-grained graded subtasks, giving dense partial-credit scoring instead of pass/fail-only grading.
Tasks are genuinely long: typically hundreds of episodes and ~85 minutes of execution, averaging 9.9M tokens per task.
Best of 15 frontier models tested hits only 15.2% pass@1 at a 0.95 partial-reward threshold, 10.9% at a perfect (1.0) threshold.
Mean pass rate across all 15 models is just 4.3% (partial) / 1.7% (perfect) — most agents barely dent these tasks.
content_html: Most terminal-agent benchmarks finish in minutes and score only the final outcome. Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench does neither: its 46 tasks run for hours and are graded on partial progress along the way — and the results show today's best agents still struggle badly with sustained work.
extra_html: Zongxia Li and colleagues built 46 long-horizon terminal tasks across nine categories — experiment reproduction, software engineering, multimodal analysis, interactive games, and scientific computing among them — each decomposed into fine-grained graded subtasks so evaluation captures how far an agent gets, not just whether it finishes. Tasks demand real endurance: on average, an agent burns 9.9M tokens over roughly 231 episodes and 85.3 minutes per task. Evaluating 15 frontier models, the single best model reaches only 15.2% pass@1 at a 0.95 partial-reward threshold and 10.9% at a perfect 1.0 threshold — while the mean across all 15 models is just 4.3% and 1.7% respectively. The authors also analyze recurring failure modes, arguing there's substantial headroom left before agents can reliably handle long, open-ended terminal work. Zongxia Li and colleagues, arXiv, July 2026.

related.title: TUA-Bench: Benchmarking General-Purpose Terminal Agents
related.hook: 120 real terminal tasks — from email triage to PhD-level scientific workflows — show even Claude Opus 4.8 tops out around 66%, far from reliable general computer use.

related.title: Failure as a Process: An Anatomy of CLI Coding Agent Trajectories
related.hook: A 3,843-trajectory autopsy of coding agents finds most failures aren't slips — they're wrong beliefs formed in the first few steps, invisible until it's too late to recover.

related.title: DocOps: Benchmarking Agents That Edit Real Documents
related.hook: Even frontier agents can't reliably edit complex documents: a verifiable benchmark pins the failures on three modes — state-tracking collapse, shallow verification, and destructive metadata edits.

flashcards.prompt: Why does Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench grade tasks differently from prior terminal benchmarks?
flashcards.back_html: It decomposes each of its 46 tasks into fine-grained graded subtasks, giving dense partial-credit scores instead of only pass/fail on the final outcome.

flashcards.prompt: How does the single best of 15 frontier models perform at the strict, perfect-reward (1.0) threshold?
flashcards.explanation_html: Even the strongest tested model reaches only 10.9% pass@1 at the perfect-reward threshold (15.2% at the looser 0.95 partial-reward threshold).

flashcards.prompt: How demanding are Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench tasks in practice?
flashcards.back_html: They typically take hundreds of episodes and about 85 minutes of execution, consuming roughly 9.9M tokens per task on average.

flashcards.prompt: What's the mean pass rate across all 15 tested models at the perfect-reward (1.0) threshold?
flashcards.explanation_html: Averaged across all 15 models, the mean pass rate is 4.3% at the partial-reward threshold and just 1.7% at the perfect-reward threshold.
